title: The ULTIMATE PPL Program (Doom Slayer Physique)
summary: NH presents a free 6-day pull/push/legs hypertrophy program modelled on the Doom Slayer's 'tank' physique, built on mirror days, interchangeable mirror lifts, supersets and heavy isolation work. He first defends PPL against its bad reputation, blaming strength-centric, compound-only implementations, then walks through every day, the rep ranges and weekly set totals.
claims: PPL's bad reputation is mostly unwarranted and comes from people who don't know how to program it
PPL can be run 3 or 6 times a week; high frequency allows lots of volume and steady progression because movement patterns are trained often
PPL lets you hit each muscle twice a week and stay fresh if programmed well
PPL's strength is synergy: days are organised by movement function, unlike bro-split pairings such as chest and legs that make no sense
The real problem with PPL is that it was turned into a rigid, repetitive strength template (deadlift, bench, squat) causing boredom and burnout
Most PPL programs over-focus on compounds and lack arm isolation, producing unbalanced physiques
Training so much that you must hold back intensity to survive the next day is poor planning and frequency scheduling, not an inherent PPL flaw
Mirror days: the 3 days repeat with identical muscle activation but different movements to reduce boredom and overuse injuries
Isolation lifts are less fatiguing than compounds, so they can be packed into every day alongside compounds
If you run PPL you should train about 6 times a week; if you want more recovery, run full body instead
This program is for intermediate and advanced lifters with good work capacity, not beginners
Rest days are flexible: take one after the first 3-day cycle if recovery struggles; you can run PPL-rest-PPL or six straight days
Novices wanting 3 days a week are better served by a full-body program than by running half of this PPL
Doom Slayer priorities: 1) shoulders, chest, back; 2) biceps, triceps, forearms; 3) posterior chain, abs, neck; 4) quads, lats, calves de-prioritised
Prioritising arms ensures compounds don't devour the whole program
Abs don't need 15-20 weekly sets; trained weighted and properly they grow a thick six-pack
People who have never trained neck will be shocked how fast it grows on little volume
Run this program on a bulk because it is extremely energy-demanding; the Doom Slayer physique is a higher-bodyfat look
Best suited to people who can sleep a lot, have low stress and can dedicate lots of time to the gym
Order the days pull-push-legs-pull-push-legs (not push-pull-legs) to separate pull and leg days as much as possible for recovery
Barbell/T-bar rows should be somewhat full-body: don't be too strict, don't cheat too much, let the posterior chain help
Use straps on rows and all back exercises to save grip for the forearm work
Supersets exist to save time and are arranged so they don't impair performance; separate them if equipment isn't available
You can never get enough traps to look like the Doom Slayer
Mirror lifts: pick one option per slot and stick with it at first; only add the alternatives when needed to keep progressing
An intermediate should already have more than one lift per muscle group
Starting push day with a press doesn't hurt the rear-delt superset because the rear delts weren't the muscle pressing
Leg days make or break PPL; people overdo them. Legs just need intensity and progression, not a million sets
Legs are kept short so you can come back the next day for pull; 80-90% of the results come from this volume
Weighted pull-ups after leg day decompress the spine; done 3x3-5, very low volume and intense
If a pull-up plus face-pull superset kills performance, your work capacity or cardiovascular fitness is poor
Kroc rows and Meadows rows train such similar muscles that you can alternate them week to week without interrupting progression
Understanding lines of specificity lets you add tons of variety to PPL without damaging progression
A proper back day is one vertical pull, one horizontal pull and one shrug pattern; 6-7 back exercises is bro-split garbage
Preacher and incline curls are easy to plateau on; a wide 6-12 range lets you taste intensity at 6 reps and move up in weight
Alternate which pattern opens each mirror day (horizontal vs vertical) so every pattern gets priority once a week
The Smith machine is great for JM presses, and the SSB bar seems built for them
You can progress RDLs and good mornings on just 2 sets
Leg days spare the lower back because on PPL low-back fatigue is split between pulling from the floor and training legs
Wrist extensions are trained because most people do lots of flexion and little extension, which can hurt elbow health and forearm development
Don't switch variations out of frustration with a plateau; repeating a weight is your body fighting. Only add a variation if you truly can't break the plateau
Lifts from mirror days can be interchanged (e.g. Kroc rows on pull 1), but avoid this at the start
Weekly sets: 20 back, 18 shoulders (excluding horizontal presses), 13 chest, 13 biceps, 8 triceps long head, 15 forearms, 15 posterior chain, 10 abs, 9 neck, 9 quads, 7 lats, 6 calves

Chest grows well from limited sets if training is intense, especially with compounds
Information and programs should be free to produce bigger naturals who enjoy their training
